comments.text:
It is fascinating to observe how human beings perceive seasonal changes as though they were unexpected revelations rather than predictable consequences of Earth's orbital mechanics and axial tilt. Approximately twenty degrees ago, metaphorically speaking, society was celebrating the phenomenon popularly labelled “hot girl summer.” Now, as autumn approaches, the same individuals appear to be embracing pumpkin patches, seasonal aesthetics, and entirely different cultural rituals.

From a scientific perspective, this transition is hardly mysterious. Earth's axial tilt of approximately 23.5 degrees, combined with its revolution around the Sun, produces seasonal variations in daylight and solar energy across much of the planet. However, the apparent transformation in human behaviour is arguably more interesting than the astronomical mechanism itself.

Human preferences are influenced by environmental conditions, social trends, psychological associations, and cultural expectations. The same individual who enjoys summer activities may develop an entirely different set of preferences when temperatures decrease and seasonal traditions become socially prominent. This is not necessarily hypocrisy; it may simply represent behavioural adaptation to changing circumstances.

Yet the internet has an extraordinary ability to document these transitions and present them as contradictions. A person enjoying one aesthetic during summer and another during autumn becomes the subject of humorous observation, despite the fact that human preferences are rarely static.

Consider the psychological dimension: seasonal activities can function as social signals, allowing individuals to participate in shared cultural experiences. Pumpkin patches, autumn photographs, and seasonal clothing are not merely activities; they can also represent belonging, nostalgia, and the desire to participate in a collective atmosphere.

Of course, the irony remains entertaining. Humanity possesses the technological capacity to calculate planetary motion with extraordinary precision, yet we continue to behave as though the arrival of autumn has personally interrupted our previous identities.

Perhaps the real phenomenon worth studying is not the changing season, but the remarkable flexibility of human identity under changing social and environmental conditions.

Sincerely, an observer of planetary mechanics who has somehow turned pumpkin patches into a study of behavioural psychology.

This was honestly one of the most unfunny things I've watched in a long time, and I don't say that lightly. I went into it expecting there to be some kind of payoff eventually, because that's usually how comedy works. Even if a joke starts slowly, there's normally a point where everything clicks together and the buildup finally makes sense. Throughout the entire video, I kept waiting for that moment to arrive. I figured maybe the opening was intentionally awkward to set up something bigger, or maybe there was going to be an unexpected twist that would completely change how I looked at everything that came before it. Instead, that moment never arrived.
The entire experience felt like one long setup without any real conclusion. Every time I thought the punchline was about to happen, the video simply continued in the same direction. It kept introducing moments that seemed like they were supposed to be leading somewhere, but none of them ever paid off. It's almost like reading a mystery novel that spends hundreds of pages building suspense only to end without revealing who committed the crime. You're left feeling less confused about the story itself and more confused about why so much time was spent building expectations that were never fulfilled.
One of the biggest problems is the pacing. Comedy relies heavily on timing, and timing is often what separates something that's genuinely hilarious from something that just feels awkward. Here, the pacing never seemed to find a rhythm. Certain moments dragged on far longer than they needed to, while other moments rushed by without giving anything enough room to become funny. Instead of creating anticipation, the extended pauses and repeated bits made everything feel slower and slower as the video went on.
As I watched, I found myself constantly thinking, "Okay, maybe the next part is where it gets funny." That thought repeated itself over and over. Every new scene felt like it was introducing another opportunity for the joke to finally land. Unfortunately, every one of those opportunities passed without anything memorable happening.

​Ingredients & Recipe:
Chicken & Rice: 2 pounds bone-in chicken pieces cut into medium-sized portions, and 2 cups long-grain basmati rice rinsed thoroughly until the water runs clear, drained, and soaked in water for 30 minutes.
​Aromatics & Veggies: 2 large finely sliced yellow onions, 1 tablespoon minced garlic, 1 tablespoon minced ginger, and 3 split green chilies sautéed in oil or ghee over medium heat for 8-10 minutes until deeply golden brown and crisp (with half saved for layering).
​Base & Spices: 1 tablespoon garam masala, 1 tablespoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon ground cumin, ½ teaspoon ground turmeric, 1 cinnamon stick, 4 crushed cardamom pods, and 4 cloves stirred into the aromatics for 1 minute to bloom, followed by half a cup of beaten yogurt.
​Liquid & Simmer: 1½ cups hot water poured into the pot with the chicken, brought to a rolling boil, then covered and simmered on medium heat for 15-20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the masala is rich and thick.
​Sear & Rest: Chicken pieces tossed with salt, turmeric, and a spoonful of yogurt, seared in 2 tbsp oil or ghee for 5-6 minutes over medium-high heat until lightly browned before starting the onions, then set aside on a clean plate to lock in the juices.
​Combine & Serve: Partially cooked, fluffy basmati rice layered over the tender chicken masala, sprinkled with the reserved fried onions, fresh mint, coriander, and a splash of saffron milk, then tightly covered and "dum" cooked on very low heat for 15-20 minutes before gently fluffing and serving hot.
​What NOT to do: Do not skip soaking the basmati rice or the grains will break during layering, do not rush the dum cooking process or the flavors won't meld together, do not add too much water to the chicken or the biryani will turn soggy, and do not stir aggressively after layering or the rice grains will snap.
